related_questions.question: What is the difference between I-130 and I-485?

text_blocks.snippet: Form I-130, Petition for Alien Relative, establishes the relationship between a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident and their foreign relative who seeks to immigrate. Form I-485, Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status, is used by individuals already in the U.S. to apply for a green card (lawful permanent resident status). Essentially, I-130 is the first step in proving the family relationship, while I-485 is the application to actually get the green card if the beneficiary is already in the U.S.
snippet_highlighted_words: I-130 is the first step in proving the family relationship, while I-485 is the application to actually get the green card if the beneficiary is already in the U.S

list.title: Purpose:
list.snippet: To establish a qualifying relationship between a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident (the petitioner) and a foreign relative who wishes to immigrate to the United States.

list.title: Who files:
list.snippet: U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents file this form on behalf of their qualifying relatives.

list.title: Relationship Examples:
list.snippet: Examples include spouses, parents, children, and siblings (depending on the petitioner's status and the specific category).

list.title: Outcome:
list.snippet: Approval of the I-130 petition means USCIS acknowledges the qualifying relationship, but it does not grant any immigration status.

list.title: Next Step:
list.snippet: After I-130 approval, the foreign relative may proceed with applying for an immigrant visa (if outside the U.S.) or adjust their status to permanent resident (if in the U.S. and eligible).

text_blocks.snippet: Form I-485 (Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status):

list.title: Purpose:
list.snippet: To apply for lawful permanent resident status (green card) for individuals who are already physically present in the United States.

list.title: Who files:
list.snippet: Individuals who are in the U.S. and meet certain eligibility requirements, often based on a previously approved I-130 petition or other qualifying basis.

list.title: Eligibility:
list.snippet: Requires proof of legal entry into the U.S., valid immigration status, and meeting other specific criteria.

list.title: Outcome:
list.snippet: Approval of the I-485 grants the individual permanent resident status in the U.S.

list.title: Filing Together (Concurrent Filing):
list.snippet: In many cases, especially for immediate relatives of U.S. citizens, I-130 and I-485 can be filed concurrently (at the same time). This can streamline the overall process.

list.title: Filing Separately:
list.snippet: If the foreign relative is outside the U.S., the I-130 is filed first. After approval, they apply for an immigrant visa at a U.S. embassy or consulate (consular processing).

list.title: Timeline:
list.snippet: Concurrent filing can potentially shorten the overall processing time, but the I-130 approval is usually a prerequisite for I-485 approval.

list.title: Eligibility:
list.snippet: Not everyone who has an approved I-130 is eligible to file I-485. The foreign relative must also be physically present in the U.S. and meet other specific criteria.

text_blocks.snippet: Form G-1145, also known as the E-Notification of Application/Petition Acceptance, is a form used by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to request electronic notifications (email or text) when an application or petition is accepted for processing. It's a one-page form that can be included with an immigration application to receive confirmation that the application has been received and accepted by USCIS.
snippet_highlighted_words: a form used by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to request electronic notifications (email or text) when an application or petition is accepted for processing

list.title: Purpose:
list.snippet: Form G-1145 is used to request email and/or text message notifications from USCIS when they accept an application or petition.

list.title: How it works:
list.snippet: When you file an application or petition with USCIS, you can include Form G-1145. If USCIS accepts your application, they will send an e-notification (either by email or text message) to the contact information you provided on the form.

list.title: Notification:
list.snippet: The e-notification will contain your receipt number (found on your I-797C form) and instructions on how to track your case status online.

list.title: Not a continuous update:
list.snippet: It's important to note that Form G-1145 provides only a one-time notification upon acceptance. For ongoing case updates, you will need to create a myUSCIS account and enable case status alerts online, according to TRW Law Firm in Bangladesh.

list.title: No additional documents:
list.snippet: Form G-1145 itself doesn't require any supporting documents beyond the information you provide on the form.

list.title: Where to find the form:
list.snippet: You can download Form G-1145 from the USCIS website.

text_blocks.snippet: Form I-193, Application for Waiver of Passport and/or Visa, is used by nonimmigrant aliens seeking admission to the United States to request a waiver of passport and/or visa requirements due to unforeseen emergencies. It can also be used by returning lawful permanent residents (LPRs) who have temporarily traveled abroad and need a waiver of documentary requirements.
snippet_highlighted_words: used by nonimmigrant aliens seeking admission to the United States to request a waiver of passport and/or visa requirements due to unforeseen emergencies

list.snippet: Purpose: To request a waiver of passport and/or visa requirements.
Who uses it: Nonimmigrant aliens and returning LPRs.
When it's used: When an individual encounters an unforeseen emergency or has a legitimate reason for not having the required documents.
Where it's filed: At the port of entry or during the immigration process.
Fee: A fee of $695 (USD) is generally required, but can be waived on a case-by-case basis by a CBP officer.
Authority: Sections 212(a)(7), 212(d)(4), and 212(k) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, as amended.
Examples: A medical emergency, loss of documents within 48 hours of departure, or a situation where a visa was cancelled.
